lede: Data feeds deliver the same row twice more often than you'd think, and every copy inflates a count or a revenue total. `distinct` removes rows that are exact copies; `dropDuplicates` can also keep one row per key, such as one row per order.
objectives: Remove exact duplicate rows with `distinct()` or `dropDuplicates()`
Keep one row per key with `dropDuplicates(["col", ...])`
Predict which rows count as duplicates, including rows with missing values
Know that Spark doesn't promise which copy `dropDuplicates` keeps, and plan for it

blocks.md:
The shop's `orders` and `order_items` are loaded as DataFrames with those names, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`. The lesson tables are clean, so the first examples build a small feed with the kinds of repeats a real export has: an order sent twice, an order with no total sent twice, and an order whose status changed and was sent again.

`df.distinct()` keeps one copy of each row and drops exact repeats. `df.dropDuplicates()` with no arguments does the same. Two rows are copies only when **every** column matches.

blocks.title: Exact copies
blocks.code:
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

schema = "order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_date DATE, status STRING, channel STRING, total DECIMAL(10,2)"
feed = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("O00001", "C0001", date(2026, 6, 11), "paid", "store", Decimal("117.99")),
    ("O00002", "C0001", date(2026, 3, 11), "delivered", "app", Decimal("79.96")),
    ("O00001", "C0001", date(2026, 6, 11), "paid", "store", Decimal("117.99")),
    ("O00003", "C0002", date(2026, 8, 28), "paid", "app", None),
    ("O00003", "C0002", date(2026, 8, 28), "paid", "app", None),
    ("O00002", "C0001", date(2026, 3, 11), "refunded", "app", Decimal("79.96")),
], schema)

print(feed.count(), "rows in the feed")
print(feed.distinct().count(), "after distinct")
print(feed.dropDuplicates().count(), "after dropDuplicates")
blocks.note: The two copies of O00001 become one, and so do the two copies of O00003. Missing values count as matching here: two `NULL` totals are treated as the same. O00002 appears twice with different statuses, so both rows stay.

blocks.md: Often what you want is one row per **key**, such as one row per `order_id`, even when other columns differ. Pass the key columns as a list: `df.dropDuplicates(["order_id"])`. It keeps every column, but only one row for each key.

blocks.title: One row per order
blocks.code:
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

schema = "order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_date DATE, status STRING, channel STRING, total DECIMAL(10,2)"
feed = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("O00001", "C0001", date(2026, 6, 11), "paid", "store", Decimal("117.99")),
    ("O00002", "C0001", date(2026, 3, 11), "delivered", "app", Decimal("79.96")),
    ("O00002", "C0001", date(2026, 3, 11), "refunded", "app", Decimal("79.96")),
], schema)

one_each = feed.dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
print(one_each.count(), "rows")
print(one_each.columns)
print(sorted(row["order_id"] for row in one_each.head(10)))
blocks.note: Two rows, one per order, with all six columns. But which O00002 survived, `delivered` or `refunded`? **Spark doesn't promise.** It can change with the data and the number of partitions.

blocks.md:
That last point matters. Use `dropDuplicates` on a key when the copies agree on everything you're going to use, or when any copy will do. If you need a particular one, like the latest status, you have to say which; later lessons show how to rank rows within a key and keep the first.

When you only need the key columns themselves, `select` them and call `distinct()`: the result can't depend on which copy was kept.

blocks.title: Which products are in each order?
blocks.code:
pairs = order_items.select("order_id", "product_id")

print(order_items.count(), "order lines")
print(pairs.distinct().count(), "different order and product pairs")
print(order_items.dropDuplicates(["order_id", "product_id"]).count(), "rows after dropDuplicates on the pair")
blocks.note: Some orders list the same product on two lines (O00001 has P005 at two prices), so 32 lines hold 27 pairs. Both ways count 27, but `dropDuplicates` also keeps `quantity` and `unit_price` from whichever line it picked.

blocks.title: A key that isn't in a list
blocks.note: `dropDuplicates` takes a list of column names, even for one column: `orders.dropDuplicates(["customer_id"])`.

concept.prompt: Two rows have the same `order_id` but different `status`. What does `distinct()` do with them?
choices: Keeps both, because not every column matches
concept.why: `distinct` removes only exact copies, where every column matches. To keep one row per order, use `dropDuplicates(["order_id"])`.

concept.prompt: Two rows are identical except that both have a missing `total`. Does `distinct()` treat them as copies?
choices: Yes: for removing duplicates, two missing values count as the same
No: a comparison with a missing value is never true
Only if you call fillna first
concept.why: `distinct` and `dropDuplicates` treat missing values as equal to each other, so the two rows become one. This differs from `==` in a filter.

concept.prompt: An order appears twice with statuses `delivered` and `refunded`. Which one does `dropDuplicates(["order_id"])` keep?
choices: Always the first one in the file
Either: Spark doesn't promise which copy it keeps
concept.why: `dropDuplicates` keeps one row per key but makes no promise about which. If you need a particular row, you have to choose it explicitly.

review: `distinct()` and `dropDuplicates()` remove exact copies: every column must match.
When removing duplicates, two missing values count as the same.
`dropDuplicates(["key", ...])` keeps one row per key, with every column. The key is always a list.
Spark doesn't promise which copy `dropDuplicates` keeps; use it when the copies agree on what you need.
To get just the keys, `select` them and call `distinct()`.
